newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - March 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - March 5.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Wednesday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan defended his warnings about stock prices, telling Congress that the Fed considers financial market conditions when setting monetary policy.
* The Dow industrials dropped 66.20 points to 6,852.72. The Treasury's bellwether 30-year bond fell 14/32 to yield 6.86, and the dollar rallied.
* UAL Corp sparked a rally in airline stocks after issuing a bullish forecast predicting first quarter earnings should exceed $1.30 per fully distributed share.
* Toyota Motor said U.S. light vehicle sales rose 17 percent in February, but Ford Motor said sales fell 3 percent.
* New home sales soared 8.6 percent in January, and the index of leading economic indicators rose 0.3 percent.
* Retailers Dayton Hudson and Federated Department Stores posted fourth quarter earnings that exceeded Wall Street expectations.

* Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat told China it needs to cut its trade surplus with the United States and gave Chinese officials with a list of major infrastructure projects that he said U.S. companies should be considered for.
* Ticketmaster is targeting as many as 7,500 operators of public U.S. golf courses in a new effort to persuade them to use its ticket-selling technology in reserving tee times.

* Winter storms that ravaged eight U.S. states will create tens of thousands of damage claims, but much of the costs will fall to the federal government's flood-insurance program rather than private-sector insurers.
* CNA Financial said two top executives of its life insurance unit have resigned after two female employees complained about harassing comments.
* A California comsumer reserach company said sales of Macintosh-style computers in key business markets grew for the second month in a row.
* Coffee futures rose nearly 7 percent, reaching their highest levels since 1994.
* Fidelity Investments has backed away from a controversial plan to pull some of its most popular funds out of the networks run by discount brokerage operations such as Charles Schwab.
* Viacom posted a fourth net loss of $0.68 per share after charges related to discontinued operations, but its results before charges exceeded Wall Street expectations.
* WHX posted a fourth quarter loss of $34.6 million and said it expects to post a loss for the current quarter because of a steelworkers' strike.
* General Electric and Massachusettes insurance regulators are negotiating a settlement that would let an insolvent insurance company with ties to GE remain in Bermuda.
* Remember when banks swore off all those crazy real-estate lending practices that got them into so much trouble in the 1980s?

Then, it was the loosening of lending standards for commercial real-estate loans that led to huge losses. Now, it may be happening again - this time with residential mortgage. Analysts warn that the most aggressive lenders - the so-called subprime lenders, who target borrowers with troubled credit histories - are leading bigger banks, like Citicorp and Chase Manhattan Bank, to loosen their home-lending standards as well. -- Heard on the Street.
* Bond prices slumped in afternoon trading yesterday as strong economic data and a lack of buying interest sent bonds lower for the seventh consecutive day. -- Credit Markets.
